The lantern room at the top of the tower smelled of brass polish, whale oil, and the dry, ancient salt that clung to every surface three hundred miles from any continent. Julian adjusted the mantle. The flame inside was not yellow or white, but a soft, impossible violet that cast no shadow against the curved glass walls.

Outside, the ocean was too still. It didn't roll with the heavy, muscular surge of the Atlantic or the long, green swells of the Pacific. It lay like black glass beneath a sky empty of stars, stretching toward an horizon that had never been mapped because maps required a shore on the other side, and here, there was none.

This was the Light at the End of Things.

Ships did not come here to avoid reefs. There were no reefs. Ships came here when they were finished being ships.

Julian had been the Keeper for forty years, though time had a habit of flattening out in the salt air until thirty years felt like a Tuesday and a single afternoon stretched into a decade. He was paid in flour, salt pork, tea, and silence—delivered once every seven years by a vessel that had no crew, only a wind that blew precisely toward the dock and then vanished.

His duty was simple: keep the lens clear, turn the crank that rotated the brass gears, and ensure the violet beam swept its slow, three-minute arc across the dark glass of the sea. When something was ready to depart, the beam would catch it.

In his first decade, it had mostly been small things. Languages that had uttered their last spoken word in a sun-baked desert; the final, solitary song of a bird species whose forests had been cut down to build warships; unwritten books that had died in the minds of feverish poets. They would drift into the beam of light, hover for a moment like motes of golden dust suspended in the purple glow, and then dissolve into the blank sky, released from the burden of existing.

Then came the larger things.

In the winter of his twentieth year, a three-masted schooner had appeared on the glass sea. Her sails were shredded to lace, her timber grey and salt-bleached, her name scraped from the transom by decades of ice. She bore no crew, only the quiet weight of every voyage she had ever made. Julian had stood on the iron catwalk outside the lantern room, the cold wind tugging at his wool coat, and watched as the beam struck her bow. The wood hadn't burned. It had simply unraveled, beam by beam, iron nail by iron nail, turning into silver mist until the water was clear again.

Tonight, the air felt different. It usually smelled of cold salt and oil, but tonight there was a faint, impossibly distant scent of crushed pine needles and wet asphalt after a summer rain. A human smell. A living smell.

Julian wiped his hands on his canvas apron and stepped out onto the gallery deck. The brass lantern housing groaned as the clockwork gears turned beneath his feet: *click, thrum, click, thrum.*

The beam reached out into the blackness.

A mile out, something was floating. It wasn't a ship, nor a bird, nor a cloud of forgotten words.

It was a house.

It was a small, two-story clapboard house with yellow paint peeling from the porch railings and a slate roof missing half its tiles. An iron tricycle sat on the front lawn, which drifted upon the black glass water as if it were rooted in soft earth. Through the curtained bay window on the ground floor, a warm, orange light flickered—not the cool, eternal violet of the lighthouse mantle, but the soft, mortal glow of an oil lamp.

Houses did not come here. Buildings belonged to geography; they rotted where they stood, crumbled into cellar holes, were buried by sand or overgrown by ivy. They did not drift out to the edge of the world.

Unless they were carried.

Julian reached for the heavy iron brake lever beside the housing and pulled.

The gears shrieked in protest, sparks flying from the brass teeth as the counterweights caught in their shaft. The lantern stopped. The violet beam froze, pinning the yellow house in a column of pale purple illumination.

Julian hurried down the spiral iron staircase—one hundred and eighty-four steps down to the stone landing. He unbolted the heavy oak door and stepped out onto the wet granite dock.

The house had drifted closer, riding the motionless water without a ripple. On the front porch, the screen door creaked open, and a woman stepped out. She wore a faded blue cardigan pulled tight around her shoulders. Her hair was silver, tied loosely at the nape of her neck.

"Is this where it goes?" she asked across the quiet water.

"Where what goes?" Julian called back.

"The place," she said, gesturing to the porch. "He built this in sixty-four. We painted it yellow twice. The roof leaked every November, no matter how many times he climbed up there with the tar."

"Who?" Julian asked.

"Everyone," she said softly. "They're all gone now. The children moved to cities with glass towers. He died in the spring when the cherry trees were in blossom. I stayed until I couldn't remember which room was which anymore." She looked down at her hands. They were translucent, like thin porcelain held up to a candle. "I thought if I stayed inside, it would stay too. But this morning I opened the front door, and the street was gone."

Julian understood. The house hadn't been abandoned. It had been remembered so fiercely by a single soul that when she finally let go, the memory had nowhere else on Earth to sink.

"You don't have to hold it anymore," Julian said gently.

She looked up at the great frozen beam above them, then stepped off the porch. She walked across the black water toward the dock. As she walked, the house behind her began to loosen its form—clapboards turning into silver dust, slate tiles floating upward like moths into the purple beam.

She reached the granite pier and looked at Julian. "Thank you, Keeper."

"It's my work," he said.

She walked past him into the shadow of the tower door. As she touched the stone threshold, she dissolved into a warm, brilliant gold that swept up through the spiral stairs, into the lantern room, and out into the empty night.

Julian returned to the top of the tower and released the brake. The gears caught again: *click, thrum, click, thrum.* The violet beam resumed its slow, three-minute sweep across the dark glass sea, where nothing remained but the endless, patient quiet.
